tips.text: Hungarian bollards are black-and-white, wedge-shaped, and typically have a **red** reflector at the front, and a white reflector at the back. [Blue reflectors](https://www.google.com/maps/@47.826971,20.8472466,3a,15y,282.66h,79.6t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s9lVB-fYRUINpTrMAYWvYZg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) are also somewhat common.
tips.note: [Croatian bollards](https://www.google.se/maps/@44.9117293,15.1630293,3a,17.5y,144.5h,72.84t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sQHfQsXnyjPhm0AakdfHr0A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) are very similar. They do, however, typically have the reflector closer to the top, and appear somewhat [thinner](https://www.google.se/maps/@44.9122903,15.1621345,3a,48.7y,222.73h,52.12t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sbWEK8Fssx79YL61MpgzMqg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) than in Hungary.

tips.text: The most common type of utility pole in Hungary is a **concrete holey pole**, with relatively thin holes going all the way down to the ground. Wooden poles are also somewhat common.
tips.note: In eastern Europe, Poland and Romania also commonly use holey poles. [Polish holey poles](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.9926761,18.7114721,3a,55.1y,130.81h,98.23t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sHtPKStzKxeiHUY1s-iNu-w!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) typically do not have holes down by the ground, and tend to be relatively thin. [Romanian holey poles](https://goo.gl/maps/QyJwGvUuzdnJLVBv5) normally either have much wider, or much taller holes.

tips.text:
Hungarian chevrons are **white on red**.

[Black-and-white](https://www.google.com/maps/@47.2517674,16.9392096,3a,37.6y,261.49h,65.38t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1s_Vx5ThXqoem-sKrW96OMFw!2e0!5s20111101T000000!7i13312!8i6656) chevrons may also be seen, but are considerably less common.
Hungarian street names typically end with the word “**utca**”. The word “út” is also used for bigger roads. These two words are unique to Hungarian, and translate to “street.”

These **green kilometre markers** can be seen along most Hungarian roads.

On highways, the numbers correspond to the ones seen on the map in small yellow boxes near exits.
Hungarian sign posts commonly appear to be **abnormally tall**, often taller than the Street View camera.
Hungarian signs are usually bolted to the sign post using **four bolts**, going through the sign, in the shape of a tall rectangle.
tips.note: This is not common in any other Eastern European countries.

tips.text:
Hungarian pedestrian crossing signs have **five stripes**. The person is wearing a **belt**. There is also a second, less common, type with four stripes and the person holding a bag.

The belt is located noticeably **low** on the person’s body, almost as if the person is sagging his pants. This is unique to Hungary.
tips.note: Among neighbouring countries, Croatia and Slovakia also have five stripes and a belt.

tips.text: Apart from European highways, there are two types of numbered roads in Hungary; roads marked with **green signs**, and highways beginning with the letter ‘**M**’, marked with **blue signs**. These road numbers are contained within a small shield shape on the sign.
Most directional signs are green, having a white inner border and a green outer border. Directional signs on M-numbered highways are blue, having a white inner border and a blue outer border.
It is somewhat common to see a small, grey flag on the antenna of Generation 3 Google cars in Hungary.
tips.note: This is also seen in the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria.

tips.text: A white generation 4 Google car can also rarely be found in Hungary.
tips.note: It can also be found in other European countries.

tips.text: A black generation 4 car that will never have an antenna can be found in Hungary.
tips.note: A black car can be found in many European countries, though it will often have an antenna visible.

tips.text: The majority of Generation 3 coverage in Hungary was taken **during winter**, resulting in very grey, dead looking coverage.
tips.note: This is also common in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria.

tips.text: Hungarian houses are typically made of stone, painted in a light colour and almost always with **red tiled roofs**. Suburban houses are typically only one storeyed, while more central houses may be taller. Houses in town and city centres are often fairly old but well-kept.
While Hungarian road lines are all-white, lines on **bicycle lanes** are typically **yellow**.
If you see a street sign with a **thick metal frame** around it, you are very likely to be in the **western** parts of the country.
If you see a **blue** or **green** street sign shaped like an **arrow**, attached to a utility pole or street light, you are likely to be in the county of Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg.
tips.note: Blue arrow-shaped street signs can also be found in [Dunakeszi](https://www.google.com/maps/@47.6290186,19.1549932,3a,29.7y,151.87h,90.55t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1se_1iRMK0jnxi0R13E9x-8A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192), north of Budapest. However, those are attached to blue sign posts.

tips.text: While the southeastern parts of Hungary are extremely flat, with almost no noticeable hills, the northern and western parts mainly consist of **forested hills and mountains**. The tallest mountains are found in the north, while the southwestern mountains are generally slightly lower.

Lake Balaton is one of the largest lakes on mainland Europe, and the **only large lake** visible on street view in Hungary. The area surrounding the lake is moderately hilly, fairly built up and a big tourist destination, with a much higher density of small hotels than almost anywhere else in the country.
Unlike most of the Hungarian plains, which is almost entirely cultivated land, the Puszta, centred around Hortobágy National Park, mainly consists of barren and wet, natural grasslands.
The road east of Tornanadaska, right by the border to Slovakia, can be easily recognized by the **snow **on and along the road, combined with the bollards and the railway right next to the road.
